## Abstract

Machine learning approaches to potential generation for molecular dynamics (MD)

simulations of low-temperature plasma-surface interactions could greatly extend the

range of chemical systems that can be modeled. Empirical potentials are difficult to

generalize to complex combinations of multiple elements with interactions that might

include covalent, ionic and metallic bonds. This work demonstrates that a specific

machine learning approach, Deep Potential Molecular Dynamics (DeepMD), can gen-

erate potentials that provide a good model of plasma etching in the Si-Cl-Ar system.

Comparisons are made between MD results using DeepMD models and empirical po-

tentials, as well as experimental measurements. Pure Si properties predicted by the

DeepMD model are in reasonable agreement with experimental results. Simulations

of Si bombardment by Ar+ ions demonstrate the ability of the DeepMD method to

predict sputtering yields as well as the depth of the amorphous-crystalline interface.

Etch yields as a function of flux ratio and ion energy for simultaneous Cl2 and Ar+

impacts are in good agreement with previous simulation results and experiment. Pre-

dictions of etch yields and etch products during plasma-assisted ALE of Si-Cl2-Ar are

shown to be in good agreement with MD predictions using empirical potentials and

with experiment. Finally, good agreement was also seen with measurements for the

spontaneous etching of Si by Cl atoms at 300 K. The demonstration that DeepMD

can reproduce results from MD simulations using empirical potentials is a necessary

condition to future efforts to extend the method to a much wider range of systems for

which empirical potentials may be difficult or impossible to obtain.

## I. Introduction

Low temperature nonequilibrium plasmas (LTPs) are used extensively in the manufac-

in the multi-decade process of increasing the scale of integrated circuit technology. How-

ever, continually shrinking device ‘critical dimensions’ is increasingly more challenging and

expensive, prompting the search for new device designs and architectures, which will in turn

require new materials and new methods of manufacturing, 3D heterogeneous integration,

and fabrication at the atomic scale.2 Development of novel plasma processes to meet these

demands is especially challenging, in part because the effects of plasma at surfaces – the

heart of the process – are generally difficult to measure or model.3

The continued advancement of plasma-assisted etching technologies requires a funda-

mental understanding of how plasma modifies the surfaces of the materials being etched.4–8

Therefore, well-controlled experiments and sophisticated modeling studies are needed. Molec-

ular dynamics (MD) simulations can be a powerful tool to understand reactive plasma-surface

interactions.9 Such simulations resolve the positions and velocities of a collection of atoms,

including chemical bond formation and breaking. In principle, MD methods offer an oppor-

tunity to understand the effects of reactive plasmas at surfaces in atomic scale detail.

However, MD simulations are limited by the number of atoms that can be included as

well as the time scales that can be simulated. MD simulations for this class of problem are

typically limited to a few thousand atoms, although exceptions are possible using leadership-

class computational hardware. Further, LTP-surface interactions typically last for seconds

to minutes. By contrast, MD simulations resolve the thermal and vibrational motions of

individual atoms and typical simulation times of an appropriate collection of atoms is usually

limited to several nanoseconds or perhaps microseconds.10 This extreme disparity in time

and length scales can be overcome in many cases, however, by simulating only the key species

interacting during the carefully selected periods of time in the overall process. The proper

choice of these key species and times is problem-dependent and generally is best done in

conjunction with associated experimental studies.11

for all species interacting in the simulation. The negative gradient of the potential is the

force on each atom and this force must be known to integrate the coupled equations of

motion of the collection of atoms. The most common approach to date for LTP surface

studies has been to utilize a semi-empirical potential with fitted parameters obtained by

utilizing experimental data and/or electronic structure calculations of the atoms, molecules

and material structures being simulated. The accuracy of empirical potentials is always an

issue, especially when more than three atoms are involved since this increases dramatically

the number of parameters that must be fit in an empirical potential. In principle, it is

possible to couple MD with more accurate potentials obtained from electronic structure

methods like density function theory (DFT). This approach is referred to as ‘ab initio MD’

(AIMD). This approach is unfortunately too computationally expensive for most problems of

interest in LTP plasma-surface interactions.9 The conflict between computational efficiency

and accuracy for chemically complex systems has limited the application of MD to many

important LTP problems to date.

For simulations of plasma-surface interactions, specifically for semiconductor device etch-

ing, empirical many-body potentials have been successfully applied to many systems of in-

terest. These include the Stillinger-Weber,12 Tersoff,13,14 Reactive Empirical Bond-Order

(REBO),15 and ReaxFF16 potentials. However, as noted before, the most notable limitation

is the determination of robust potential parameters, the number of which rapidly increases

as more atoms types are introduced.

In recent years, there has been a rapid increase in the use of machine learning (ML) for

the development of MD potentials. ML approaches used to generate potentials include neu-

ral network (NN) models such as the Deep Potential Molecular Dynamics (DeepMD),17,18

SchNet,19 and Neural Equivariant Interatomic Potentials (NequIP)20 frameworks; kernel-

based methods such as Gradient Domain Machine Learning (GDML)21 and Gaussian Ap-

proximation Potentials (GAP);22 and linear models such as Spectral Neighbor Analysis

Potential (SNAP),23 Moment Tensor Potential (MTP),24 and Atomic Cluster Expansion

Neural networks are ML models that provide a representation of arbitrary nonlinear

functions. The NN is trained by optimizing its parameters in order to fit a given dataset

in which the value of the function is known. In the DeepMD method,17,18 NNs are used to

represent interatomic potentials by training on ab initio quantum density functional theory

data. These potentials are then used to perform simulations using classical MD codes such

as LAMMPS26,27 and GROMACS.28 Thus, in addition to providing classical MD simula-

tions with ab initio levels of accuracy, the DeepMD method also provides a streamlined

methodology for potential development.

In the present work, we use DeepMD to generate potentials for the Si-Cl-Ar system and

study various low-temperature plasma-surface interactions by performing MD simulations.

The DeepMD method was chosen since it has been shown to provide an accurate represen-

tation of different phases of silicon. Specifically, Bonati and Parrinello developed a DeepMD

model to study nucleation of crystalline Si,29 and Li et al. predicted thermal properties of

Si using a deep potential.30 Prior applications of DeepMD include studies of the phase dia-

gram of water,31 proton transfer reactions at the water-TiO2 interface,32 liquid–liquid phase

transition in supercooled water,33 chemical reactions in molten alkali carbonate-hydroxide

electrolytes,34 structural properties of molten magnesium chloride35 and liquid silica,36 and

phase behavior and transport properties of CO2.37

A key element in plasma-surface interaction simulations is energetic ion (or fast neutral)

impacts of a surface being processed. Atoms impacted by energetic species will experience

interactions at relatively short distances. At these distances, conventional DFT calculations

may fail, since the interactions cannot be treated as quasi-static. Short range interactions

can only be accurately described by the Ziegler-Biersack-Littmark (ZBL) screened nuclear

repulsion potential.38 Further, the magnitudes of energies and forces in irradiation processes

are much larger than those in near-equilibrium systems, which may present additional diffi-

culties for NN training. Therefore, applications of ML potentials for sputtering processes are

## II. Methods

## A. Development of Deep Potential Model

The DP-GEN active learning approach of Zhang et al.46 was employed to develop a

DeepMD model for our system, including Si, Ar and Cl interactions. This procedure ensures

that the training data set is representative of all configurations that the DeepMD model

explores. The DP-GEN procedure is performed in a series of successive iterations. Each

of these iterations consists of three steps: training, exploration, and labeling, as displayed

in Figure 1. It should be noted that throughout the DP-GEN procedure, an ensemble of

models is used. These models are trained on the same data set, but different random seeds

are chosen to initialize the neural network parameters. The training process updates the

model parameters to minimize the loss function, which is a measure of energy and force

Training. In this step, an ensemble of models is generated using the Deep Potential

(DP) method,17 which is a deep neural network representation of an interatomic potential.

The DP model is illustrated in Figure 2. The DP model involves defining a local environment

for each atom i, containing its neighbors within a cut-off radius. The relative positions of

all neighbors with respect to atom i, {Rij}, are mapped to descriptors, {Dij}, through an

embedding network. This approach preserves symmetry with respect to translation, rotation,

and permutation of atoms of the same type.50 {Dij} are used as input to a fitting network,

which yields the atomic energies, Ei, as output. The total energy of a given configuration is

expressed as the sum of atomic energies: E = ∑i Ei. Atomic forces, Fi, are computed from

the negative gradient of the system energy with respect to position.

## B. Molecular Dynamics Simulations of Plasma-Surface Interactions

Simulations were performed with LAMMPS (23 Jun 2022 version)26,27 integrated with

DeePMD-kit v2.1.5,50,51 using one DeepMD model randomly selected from the previously

trained model ensemble as a LAMMPS pair style. Input data for the simulations are available

as described in the Data Availability Statement.

The MD simulation protocols and assumptions used for plasma-surface interactions have

been described in detail previously.42,43,45 Briefly, simulations consisted of a series of sequen-

tial impacts in which a particle hits a Si slab of size 32.58 ˚A × 32.58 ˚A × 54.30 ˚A, initially

in a diamond cubic lattice structure. For this system size, a monolayer corresponds to 72

Si atoms. Periodic boundary conditions were used in the x and y-directions, while in the

z-direction the Si(100) surface was exposed to a vacuum. The bottom two Si monolayers

were fixed to prevent movement in the z-direction after ion impacts. Each impact consisted

of a microcanonical (NVE) trajectory of 1 ps. Particles were placed in a random initial

position above the Si slab, at a height such that its distance from the surface is larger than

the cut-off radius of the potential. “Thermal” particles (Cl2 molecules in this work) have an

initial velocity sampled from the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution at 300 K, with a negative

z-component to ensure that they will impact the surface. Ions (Ar+ in this work) are given

an initial velocity normal to the surface corresponding to their energy. It should be noted

that the impinging Ar+ ions are modeled as neutral atoms during the bombardment process,

since it is assumed that they undergo Auger neutralization before impacting the surface.

The energy added to the system by the particle impacts causes the temperature to increase.

Therefore, after each impact, a Berendsen thermostat54 is used and the system is run at

constant temperature for 1 ps to bring the cell back to 300 K.

In a previous experimental ALE study, the flux of Cl2 molecules on the Si surface is

estimated as 9.8 × 1017 Cl2/(cm2 s) using kinetic gas theory, while the flux of Ar+ ions is

3.7 × 1016 Ar+/(cm2 s).43 Based on these values, the time between impacts on a Si surface

with the aforementioned surface area is on the order of hundreds of microseconds for Cl2

The MD simulations performed in this work can be classified into simultaneous ion and

neutral impact simulations and atomic layer etching (ALE) simulations. For the simultane-

Cl2 molecules and Ar+ ions, for different values of the flux ratio of Cl2 to Ar+ in order to

compare to experiment. This sequence simulates the simultaneous exposure of the surface

to neutral thermal Cl2 and Ar+. For the ALE simulations, Cl2 molecules impact the surface

first until the surface is saturated with Cl, then impacts by Ar+ are simulated. The Si slab

is subjected to a series of ALE cycles in order to reach a cyclic steady state condition, suit-

able for statistical analysis and comparison to experiment. Each cycle consists of a series

of thermal Cl2 impacts followed by a series of Ar+ impacts. Etch yields for simulation are

calculated when the Cl uptake on the Si surface has reached its steady state value. For

each simulation, at least 3 independent runs are performed in order to compute standard

deviations. Other details of the simulation protocols are reported in detail elsewhere.42,43,45

## IV. Concluding Remarks

Neural-network potentials created using the Deep Potential (DP) procedure for the Si-

Ar-Cl system were used to predict various plasma-surface interactions relevant to low tem-

perature plasma etching applications. The DeepMD model, which is trained on data from

quantum DFT calculations, is able to predict atomic energies and forces with near-ab ini-

tio accuracy. Pure Si properties predicted by the model are in reasonable agreement with

experimental results with the differences due to the inaccuracies in the underlying DFT.

Simulations of Si bombardment by Ar+ ions demonstrate the ability of the DeepMD method

to predict sputtering yields as well as the depth of the amorphous-crystalline interface. Etch

yield as a function of flux ratio and ion energy for simultaneous Cl2 and Ar+ impacts were

in good agreement with previous results and experiment. Predictions of etch yields and etch

products during plasma-assisted ALE of Si-Cl2-Ar were shown to be in good agreement with

MD predictions using empirical potentials and with experiment. Finally, good agreement

was also seen with measurements for the spontaneous etching of Si by Cl atoms at 300 K.

The ultimate goal is to use DeepMD to develop multi-element potentials for the many

combinations of process gases and materials of current and future interest. DeepMD models

have previously been used for systems containing four or more elements,77–80 while empirical

potentials are difficult to generalize to the complex combinations of multiple elements with
